Your mission

You are an artist who paints with code. In weeks 10, 11 and 12 you will make a Python turtle program that is a little interactive art show:

  1. it says hello to the person watching (the “viewer”),

  2. it asks them one or two questions,

  3. it draws a picture or pattern that changes because of their answers,

  4. and it has a surprise, so it is a bit different every time you run it.

In week 12 you will show it to your family at the Showcase and explain one part of your code. You can work alone or with your partner. If you work in a pair, you both need to be able to explain every part.

TipAn example

Your teacher has a finished example called Night Sky Postcard. It asks “How many stars?” and “Day or night?”, then draws the sky, a moon or a sun, random stars and a row of houses. Ask to see it, then make something that is yours.

The six ingredients

Your finished program must use all six. Check off each one when it is in your code and working.

Ingredient What it looks like in Python
☐ A question answer = input("How many fish? ")
☐ A variable fish_count = int(answer) (a labeled box that remembers)
☐ An if if mood == "happy": … else: …
☐ A loop for i in range(fish_count): …
☐ Something random x = random.randint(-350, 350)
☐ My own function def fish(x, y, color): … and then calling it: fish(0, 0, ORANGE)

Idea menu

Pick one, mix two, or invent your own. Every idea can be an artwork or a little game.

Asks “How many fish?” and “Deep or shallow?”. Your fish(x, y, color) function swims in random places.

Asks “How many flowers?” and “Sunny or rainy?”. Rain draws lines, sun draws a sun.

Asks “How many eyes?” and “Happy or grumpy?”. The if picks the mouth shape.

Asks “How many planets?”. Planets get random sizes; a rocket() function flies past.

Asks “How many sides?”. A loop turns and repeats your shape with random colors.

Asks “How much snow: a little or a lot?”. Snowflakes are made by a snowflake() function.

Asks “How many fireworks?”. Each firework is a burst of lines in a random place.

The program secretly picks a random number of sides, draws the shape, asks “How many sides?” and the if says “Correct!” or “Try again”.

SafetyYour art, your privacy

Use a nickname on your artwork, never your real full name, address or school. Do not ask the viewer for private things either: ask about colors, numbers, moods or animals instead. At the showcase we show projects on the screen only. Nothing is uploaded.

Where things go on the screen

The turtle window is 800 steps wide and 600 steps tall. The middle is (0,0)(0, 0). Use t.penup() and t.goto(x, y) to jump to a spot without drawing.

Milestones

Build in small steps. Each milestone has a check. Check it off when it is done.

Milestone Done when…
☐ M1 Plan
end of week 10		 My plan sheet is filled in and my teacher said OK. I opened my_art_show.py and saved it with my project’s name.
☐ M2 Core drawing works
week 11, first half		 My function draws my main thing, and I call it at least twice in different places. The program runs without red errors.
☐ M3 Surprise and polish
week 11, second half		 My questions, my if, my loop and my random surprise all work. A partner tested it and gave me “two stars and a wish”. I added a title or message.
☐ M4 Showcase
week 12		 I can run my program for a visitor and explain one part of my code in my own words.

TipSmall steps beat big leaps

Change one thing, press Run, look. Then change the next thing. If something breaks, you know it was the last thing you changed. Save often with Cmd + S.

How my project is assessed

Your teacher uses this rubric. Use it yourself too: circle where you are now, and again at the end. Every column is a good place to be on the way.

I can…  Just starting  Getting there  Got it  Expert
make it my own (creativity) I copied an example. I changed colors or sizes in an example. My picture has my own idea, my own function and a surprise. My idea is unique and I added extra details or a twist nobody expected.
make my code work It does not run yet. It runs, but some parts are missing or broken. It runs from start to end without errors. It also copes with odd answers (like “lots” instead of a number).
use the six ingredients I used 1 or 2. I used 3 or 4. I used all 6. I used all 6, and my function has parameters I really use (like x, y, color).
explain my code I can say what my program does. I can point to my loop and my function. I can explain how one part of my code works, line by line. I can explain why I chose it, and how I fixed a bug.

Need a different path?

TipSupport path: make it in Scratch

You can build the same art show in Scratch instead. The rubric is exactly the same, and you use the same six ingredients:

Ingredient Scratch block
A question ask … and wait, then the answer block
A variable Make a Variable, then set / change
An if if … then / if … then … else
A loop repeat … or forever
Something random pick random … to …
My own function Make a Block (a My Block, with inputs if you can)

Make your art show react while it is open. Put this before turtle.done(). Pressing the space bar adds a new star in a random place:

Key presses with onkey

def add_star():
    x = random.randint(-380, 380)
    y = random.randint(20, 280)
    t.penup()
    t.goto(x, y)
    t.dot(8, YELLOW)

screen.onkey(add_star, "space")   # no () after add_star
screen.listen()                   # start listening for keys

Click on the turtle window first, then press the key. Ideas: "c" changes the sky color, "Up" draws a firework, "r" adds rain.

Starter files

These are templates to start from. They run, but the interesting parts are yours to write.

All starter files (ZIP, 2 KB)

My Interactive Art Show - starter

This folder is where your final project begins.

How to start

  1. Open Thonny.
  2. Click File > Open... and open my_art_show.py from this folder.
  3. Click File > Save as... and give your project its own name, for example rainbow_city.py or fish_party.py. Use small letters and underscores, no spaces. Never put your real name in the file name.
  4. Press the green Run button. A window opens with an orange square. That means everything works. Now make it yours!

Remember your plan

Keep your plan sheet (from the project brief) next to the computer. It says:

  • what your program asks the viewer,
  • what it draws,
  • what your function is called and what it draws.

The six ingredients

Your finished program must use all six. The comments at the top of my_art_show.py have a checklist.

Milestones

Tips

  • Work in tiny steps: change one thing, press Run, look, then change the next thing.
  • Save often (Cmd + S).
  • Stuck for more than 5 minutes? Read the red error message out loud to your partner, then ask your teacher. Bugs are normal!
  • Want to see an example of a finished project? Ask your teacher to show you the Night Sky Postcard.

my_art_show.py

# My Interactive Art Show
# Made by: (write a nickname here - never your real full name)
#
# My idea in one sentence:
#   TODO: describe your picture or game here
#
# My program must use ALL of these ingredients. Check them off as you go:
#   [ ] input()   - asks the viewer at least one question
#   [ ] a variable - remembers an answer or a number
#   [ ] an if      - chooses what to draw from an answer
#   [ ] a loop     - for ... in range(...): repeats something
#   [ ] random     - adds a surprise
#   [ ] def        - at least one function I made myself
#
# Work in small steps: change one thing, press Run, look, then change the next.

import random
import turtle

# ===== PART 1: MY COLORS =====
# Color-blind-safe colors. Use these names instead of typing the codes.
ORANGE = "#E69F00"
SKY_BLUE = "#56B4E9"
GREEN = "#009E73"
YELLOW = "#F0E442"
BLUE = "#0072B2"
VERMILLION = "#D55E00"
PURPLE = "#CC79A7"
BLACK = "#000000"
WHITE = "#FFFFFF"

# ===== PART 2: SET UP THE SCREEN AND THE TURTLE =====
screen = turtle.Screen()
screen.setup(800, 600)          # x goes from -400 to 400, y from -300 to 300
screen.title("My Art Show")     # TODO: put the name of your artwork here

t = turtle.Turtle()
t.speed(0)                      # 0 = fastest
t.pensize(2)


# ===== PART 3: MY OWN COMMANDS (FUNCTIONS) =====
# This example function draws a square with its bottom-left corner at (x, y).
# TODO: change it into YOUR function (a flower, a fish, a robot, a star...)
#       and give it a name that says what it draws.
def my_shape(x, y, color):
    t.penup()
    t.goto(x, y)
    t.setheading(0)
    t.pendown()
    t.color(BLACK, color)
    t.begin_fill()
    for side in range(4):
        t.forward(50)
        t.left(90)
    t.end_fill()


# ===== PART 4: GREET THE VIEWER AND ASK QUESTIONS =====
print("Welcome to my art show!")    # TODO: write your own greeting

# TODO: ask your first question and keep the answer in a variable.
# Example:  answer = input("How many fish? ")
#           fish_count = int(answer)
# Remember: never ask for real names, ages, addresses or other private things.


# ===== PART 5: MAKE A CHOICE WITH IF =====
# TODO: use if / elif / else to choose something from an answer.
# Example:  if mood == "happy":
#               screen.bgcolor(YELLOW)
#           else:
#               screen.bgcolor(BLUE)


# ===== PART 6: DRAW! USE A LOOP AND RANDOM =====
# This line uses the example function once so you can see it working.
# TODO: call YOUR function inside a loop, using random places or colors.
# Example:  for i in range(5):
#               x = random.randint(-350, 350)
#               my_shape(x, 0, PURPLE)
my_shape(-25, -25, ORANGE)


# ===== PART 7: FINISHING TOUCHES =====
# TODO (optional): write a title on the screen with t.write(...),
#                  hide the turtle with t.hideturtle()

print("Thank you for visiting my art show!")
turtle.done()
